prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, in which neutral atoms trapped at a magic wavelength reach fractional uncertainties near 1e-18

statement.case_for: I keep the configuration I stated in round 1: a single part for Katori and Ye on optical lattice clocks. I opened with IceCube because I weigh a clue found in nature most heavily, and the round-1 exchange has not changed that weighting. It has changed what I think the choice is between. The lattice clock is a discovery in the sense that matters here: the magic-wavelength lattice removes the trap-induced shift while many atoms are interrogated at once, which is a new regime and not a better version of the comb or of single-ion control. The uncertainty near 1e-18, the many-body clock operation and the millimetre-scale redshift measurements have been reproduced by several laboratories over two decades, so the science is not in doubt. The credit maps onto the two names, Katori for the idea and Ye for the realisation. IceCube has the stronger claim to be a new window on nature, but nobody in the round-1 files, including me, can say which three people made the decisive contribution inside a collaboration of hundreds, and the source associations are still moving. I would rather give a prize now whose citation can be defended line by line than one whose names I could not justify. The redefinition of the second is supporting evidence for me and not a condition, because the scientific case is complete without it.
statement.case_against: My strongest reservation is unchanged. This is recognition of a measurement capability, and the committee has honoured the frequency comb in 2005 and control of single trapped ions in 2012. I answer the distinctness question with the neutral-atom ensemble in a magic-wavelength lattice, but I accept that this is a judgement and that a reasonable member could call it a refinement of an honoured line. The credit also stops short of Takamoto and the other Sr and Yb groups, and of the ion-clock community. I have no way inside the supplied record to verify the priority history, and I rely on recollection for the roles of the lattice proposers. Finally I am choosing a cleaner attribution over what may be the more consequential discovery, and if the IceCube source picture hardens, I expect to regret that this year's choice was made at the expense of B032.

responses.point: Lindroth asks whether the redefinition of the second is a condition for the prize or only supporting evidence, and whether other clock groups change the credited names.
responses.response: I treat the redefinition as supporting evidence and not as a condition. The prize would be justified by the invention and by the demonstrated 1e-18 performance whether or not the General Conference on Weights and Measures acts soon, and making the prize wait on a metrology body would put the timing of our judgement in someone else's hands. On the other groups, the supplied record does not give me grounds to widen the names beyond Katori and Ye, and with a three-person limit I cannot add Takamoto or others without a priority record that none of us has verified. I would instead answer your concern in the wording: the citation should say invention and realisation of the lattice clock, not clocks in general. I take your agreement with Mehlig that a single part is better than pairing the clocks with a cold-atom theory part, and I do not see a pairing that improves the allocation.

responses.point: Johansson moved his own view to B004 but wants the citation worded around the lattice-clock concept and its realisation at 1e-18, not around timekeeping in general, and he raises Ye as credited under other candidate lines.
responses.response: I agree with the citation point and have adopted it: my wording now names the magic-wavelength lattice and the 1e-18 level and does not claim timekeeping or time measurement as a whole. On Ye under other lines, the shortlist file shows him only under B004, so there is no balance problem and no hidden overlap to manage; that was the question the chair flagged and I regard it as settled. I welcome your move from eighth place, and I note that you moved on the physics and not on counting votes. We still differ on B023, which you keep as your first alternative. I rank it behind IceCube and graphene because the experimental realisation by Wineland, Blatt and Monroe was already partly prized in 2012, and a theory-only part would need an argument that the blueprint stands alone.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B010 as a single part for MacDonald, Jarillo-Herrero and Bistritzer, argues that the correlated states are an established discovery whatever the pairing mechanism, and names B004 as his first alternative.
responses.response: Your reading that the discovery is the correlated insulating and superconducting states, and not the pairing glue, is the strongest answer to the maturity objection, and I give it real weight. Reproduction across several groups makes the phenomenon secure. I keep B010 as my second alternative for that reason. My difficulty is that the credit is more contested than in your account: the 2011 paper is a joint prediction, the 2018 experimental result had a first author outside the three names, and earlier continuum treatments by Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto are on record. The field is eight years old and I expect the interpretation and the credit to settle within a few years. If the committee must choose now, I would ask you whether you would accept B004 as the cleaner choice and revisit twisted bilayer graphene when the mechanism is clearer.

responses.point: Kroll discloses a doctoral research stay in John Hall's laboratory at JILA, Ye's institution, and the chair asked whether this needs more than disclosure.
responses.response: I do not think Kroll's stay requires more than the disclosure he has made. A visit as a doctoral student to a laboratory in the same city as Ye, with no documented collaboration with Katori or Ye, is a historical connection to an environment, and it is already on the record. He is also one of the members who weighs the instrument side most generously, which he states himself, so I read his ranking with that in mind and I do not think it changes the argument. I would ask only that he not be the one to draft the credit wording, since he is closest to the lab where the realisation work was done. I also thank him for pressing Johansson on why the clocks were ranked eighth, which brought out the overlap concern in the open.

responses.point: Pearce, as chair, ranked B032 second and says his professional proximity to astroparticle physics means he would weigh it with care and consider recusal if it became the leading option.
responses.response: I agree with your handling of your own proximity to IceCube and I stand by what I said in round 1: the merit of B032 is a question every member can assess, and your proximity should shape who drives the case and not whether the committee discusses it. On the question of how to resolve three names for IceCube, I cannot offer a clean answer. I named Halzen, Karle and Yoshida from recollection and I accept Lindroth's point that forced to two names she would drop Yoshida, which shows that the allocation is not settled in the files. Until a member can show from the record who made the decisive contribution within the collaboration, I do not think B032 should come ahead of B004.

uncertainties: Whether the committee will accept that the magic-wavelength lattice clock is a distinct step beyond the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes, which is a judgement and not something the files can prove.
Whether Takamoto and other Sr and Yb groups, or the PTB, NIST, SYRTE and RIKEN groups, have priority claims that should change the credit. I cannot verify this from the supplied evidence.

Whether the IceCube source associations (TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068, Galactic plane) will sharpen and whether a defensible three-name allocation exists, which would change my view of B032 in a later year.
Whether the committee will find the unresolved pairing mechanism and the credit history of magic-angle graphene settled enough to return to B010 soon.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict has appeared from my profile for any shortlisted candidate, and the round-1 exchange has not changed that. My documented connections are to David Gross, Hector Rubinstein, Thomas Van Riet and the Uppsala theoretical-physics group, and none of them is among the credited names. I work in string theory, gravitation and cosmology, which is not close to the lattice-clock field. I note that Kroll has disclosed a doctoral stay in Hall's laboratory at JILA and I regard that disclosure as sufficient. I also note that as Secretary I have a role in procedure, but I do not carry any private knowledge of the committee's deliberations into this statement.
